label: SYNTHETIC READER: a test instrument, never a reader. Fictional; not evidence about the book; not readership.

findings.quote: Both read the hold the same way: part one final, not locked.
findings.why: A run of talk-team shorthand (hold, locked, five-step session, hour eighteen) in one paragraph, before the book's own terms are placed for a busy reader on a phone.

findings.quote: any member, in any session, can write the file.
findings.why: 'The file' is never named here, so the one mechanism a team could copy (a hold file anyone may write) is not clear until much later.

findings.quote: Any member may write a hold. Only I lift it, and only I restart a member's work.
findings.why: A reader whose deal-breaker is one central person needs the book to say plainly that this is a single point of failure and what the named stand-in would be, not only that one is missing.

findings.quote: That line is the whole chapter in one sentence.
findings.why: A 'that is the point' style opening that tells me what to take from the quote instead of letting the next sentences do it.

findings.quote: Draw the day as states and it is very simple.
findings.why: The figure on line 13 already draws running, held, released, and these paragraphs then read the same picture out again.

findings.quote: "A scope is a setting, not a boundary: it catches mistakes, not a steered agent."
findings.why: The same slide line is quoted at length in chapter 18 line 32 with the same gloss, so the best idea in the pair is spent twice.

findings.quote: No session ever held it. Part five is where it gets its chair.
findings.why: Chapter 6 says part four covers security's empty chair and this chapter fills the chair at its own end, so 'part five' sends me looking for the wrong place.

findings.quote: That is the point: a team of agents you cannot read is a team you cannot trust.
findings.why: A 'that is the point' opening that announces the lesson, and the preceding two short sentences make it a run of three.

findings.quote: It was lifted at my word, given in another member's session, and that session carried it out
findings.why: I cannot tell who did what; a team copying the pattern needs the stop and restart steps spelled out in order.

findings.quote: Most of the player's commits of the afternoon, and the lock tool, name no member
findings.why: 'The player' and 'the lock tool' are used as if known; as a first reader I stall on what they are.

findings.quote: Two readers who never compared notes reached the same sequence.
findings.why: The historian's line two paragraphs on (line 28) says the same thing again, and the paragraph before it already showed the agreement.

findings.quote: The record does not say whether one would have; it only shows that none had to.
findings.why: The narrator reports what the record shows instead of saying from now, in the first person, what the editor makes of it.

findings.quote: no brief, no chapter, no decision, no finding.
findings.why: A short list of four after the same device on line 9 (no timeline, no register, no chapter), so the pattern starts to feel like a habit.

findings.quote: something you expect, something that checks, or something that locks.
findings.why: A good takeaway, but it comes after nine long interviews and is the only thing a busy reader can act on tomorrow, so it is late and thin.

what_holds: 18-how-do-we-contain-this.md: the running, held, released picture is a copyable pattern for my own team, and the chapter says plainly how thin some of the controls were.
18-how-do-we-contain-this.md: the 'Something to try' card (write down who stops and who restarts before you need it) is something I could do this week.
19-a-second-team-reading-cold.md: the idea of giving finished work to someone with none of your context is simple and transferable, and the six things the blind team found make it concrete.

06-roles-as-a-cast-you-can-read.md: the plain-words page plus a checkable policy for every agent is a pattern I could copy with the agents I already have, and the list of what did not go well in each interview is honest.
notes: Read on a phone in five minutes, chapter 6 is too long for me (nine interviews) and chapter 19 leans on talk-team shorthand; chapter 18 is the one I would act on. The stop-and-restart rule depends on the editor alone, which is the deal-breaker for my team unless a named stand-in is spelled out.
